title: What do these products of brackets turn out to be?
description: A string of products starts with one minus one half and adds one more bracket each time, up to one minus one tenth. Each bracket becomes a single fraction, and the numerators and denominators cancel in a chain, so only the first numerator and the last denominator are left.
teaching_notes: One idea: each bracket one minus one over k is the fraction k minus one over k, so in the product every numerator cancels the denominator before it. Watch for students who multiply every term out instead of cancelling, or who lose track of which numerator and denominator are left.

video_script.why: A learner multiplies a long chain of fractions by cancelling, as with the six fractions of a dramma, and sees what is left.
video_script.substitution: the book's own four products, starting at one minus one half and stopping at one minus one half, one third, one fifth and one tenth
video_script.anchor: a growing string of brackets, each of the form one minus one over a number
video_script.payoff_line: The answers are one half, one third, one fifth and one tenth, and in general one over n.

final_answer.spoken: one half, one third, one fifth and one tenth, and in general one over n

video_script.fraction_reading: one half, two thirds, three quarters, four fifths, nine tenths, one third, one fifth, one tenth, one over n
maths_rules: check: every bracket is less than 1, so each product is smaller than the one before
video_script.design: The string of brackets is turned into a string of fractions; the numerators and denominators are joined by cancelling lines so the chain collapses to two numbers.

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about a string of products.
<bookmark mark='start'/>Start with one minus one half.
<bookmark mark='grow'/>Then multiply by one minus one third, then by one minus one quarter, and so on.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What do the products turn out to be, and what do you notice?

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a whole bar cut into three equal parts with one part taken away; the two parts left are labelled

marks.left: one part of the bar is crossed out
marks.whole: three thirds are shown to make one whole
marks.n: the last number is written as n

narration: <bookmark mark='left'/>One minus one third is what is left of a whole after one third is taken away.
<bookmark mark='whole'/>Three thirds make one whole, so the part left is two thirds.
<bookmark mark='n'/>The last number can be any number, so we call it n.

beats.on_screen: Given: four products, each starting at (1 − 1/2) and stopping at (1 − 1/2), (1 − 1/3), (1 − 1/5) and (1 − 1/10)

marks.given: the four products are written one below the other

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, four products, each starting at one minus one half.
They stop at one minus one half, one third, one fifth and one tenth.

beats.on_screen: To find: each product, and a general statement

marks.find: the words each product and general statement are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find each product, and then say what is true in general.

marks.bracket: each bracket is written as one fraction
marks.more: three quarters and four fifths are written
marks.last: nine tenths is written at the end of the list

narration: <bookmark mark='bracket'/>Step one, write each bracket as one fraction.
One minus one half is one half, and one minus one third is two thirds.
<bookmark mark='more'/>One minus one quarter is three quarters, and one minus one fifth is four fifths.
<bookmark mark='last'/>This goes on up to one minus one tenth, which is nine tenths.

marks.two: one half times two thirds is written
marks.cancel: the two on the top is cancelled with the two on the bottom

narration: <bookmark mark='two'/>Step two, multiply the first two brackets, one half times two thirds.
<bookmark mark='cancel'/>The two on the top cancels the two on the bottom.

beats.on_screen: 1/2 × 2/3 × 3/4 × 4/5 = (1 × 2 × 3 × 4) / (2 × 3 × 4 × 5); each numerator cancels the denominator before it; only the 1 on top and the 5 below stay

marks.four: the first four brackets are written as fractions
marks.cancel: each numerator is cancelled with the denominator before it
marks.left: the one on the top and the five on the bottom are circled

narration: <bookmark mark='four'/>Step three, take the first four brackets.
The product is one half times two thirds times three quarters times four fifths.
<bookmark mark='cancel'/>Each numerator cancels the denominator before it.
<bookmark mark='left'/>Only the one on the top and the five on the bottom stay.

beats.on_screen: 1/2 × 2/3 × 3/4 × ... × 9/10: only the 1 on top and the 10 below stay

marks.ten: the chain of nine fractions is written up to nine tenths
marks.left: the one on the top and the ten on the bottom are circled

narration: <bookmark mark='ten'/>Step four, go up to one minus one tenth.
The product is one half times two thirds, and so on, up to nine tenths.
<bookmark mark='left'/>The same thing happens. Only the one on the top and the ten on the bottom stay.

beats.on_screen: (1 − 1/2) × (1 − 1/3) × ... × (1 − 1/n) = 1/2 × 2/3 × ... × (n − 1)/n: only the 1 on top and the n below stay

marks.gen: the string is written up to one minus one over n
marks.last: the last fraction n minus one over n is written
marks.left: the one on the top and the n on the bottom are circled

narration: <bookmark mark='gen'/>Step five, in general, go up to one minus one over n.
<bookmark mark='last'/>The last fraction is n minus one over n.
<bookmark mark='left'/>Only the one on the top and the n on the bottom stay.

beats.on_screen: check: every bracket is less than 1, so each product is smaller than the one before
narration: <bookmark mark='check'/>Step six, check that the products get smaller each time.
Every bracket is less than one, so the product shrinks as more brackets join.

marks.ans: the four answers and the general statement are boxed
marks.why: the chain of cancelling lines is shown once more

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The answers are one half, one third, one fifth and one tenth, and in general one over n.
<bookmark mark='why'/>Everything cancels in a chain.
Only the first top and the last bottom are left.
